Vignette:
# Marcus Volkov

Marcus Volkov, forty-five, had spent twenty years as a foreign correspondent, chasing stories across three continents with the kind of restless hunger that his wife Elena had long ago learned to accept as part of who he was. He had covered wars in the Balkans, insurgencies in the Levant, and political upheaval in Eastern Europe—work that had made him careful, yes, but not afraid. Until March of last year, when an assignment in a country he cannot now name without his chest tightening had ended with him and two local fixers locked in a concrete basement for eleven days.

The men who took them had been methodical and clinical. They wanted information about his sources, about which officials he had spoken to, about the contents of encrypted drives. They wanted to know which stories he was planning to publish. When Marcus refused, they moved on to the others. He watched what they did to his fixers when answers didn't come fast enough. He watched and could do nothing. They kept their hands on him constantly—gripping his arm to move him, pressing a forearm across his throat when he tried to speak, holding his head down when they forced him to watch. The smell of alcohol on their breath was always there, always mixed with sweat and the staleness of the basement. One of them, the one who did most of the talking, reeked of cheap vodka. That smell became a kind of countdown in Marcus's mind, a signal that something was about to happen.

On the eighth day, one of them wrenched his neck back so hard he heard something crack. The pain was extraordinary, but what stayed with him was not the pain itself—that had faded within weeks—but the way his body now responded to any pressure there, any unexpected touch at the back of his neck or shoulders. His nervous system had learned that touch meant danger, and it had not forgotten.

When he was finally released—traded for something, he never fully understood what—Marcus told himself he would be fine. He had survived. He had not given them what they wanted. He flew home to Elena and their apartment in Brooklyn, where he tried to resume the life that had been waiting for him. But the life he returned to was not the one he had left.

Within weeks, the memories began their relentless cycling. He would be sitting at his desk working on a piece, and suddenly he was back in the basement, the memory arriving with the same visceral terror he had felt in the moment. Not a thought about the event, but the event itself, playing through his mind like a film he could not stop or pause. The replays came without warning and with full emotional intensity—his heart would race, his breathing would shallow, and for a few seconds he would be absolutely certain he was in danger again. The rational part of his mind would catch up, would remind him he was in his apartment, that he was safe, but the delay between the terror and the cognition had become the shape of his daily life.

Sound became his constant threat monitor. Unexpected noises—a car backfiring outside, a door slamming in the building, even the sudden ring of his office phone—sent him into an immediate state of high alert. His body would tense, his attention would narrow, and he would be scanning for the source of the sound as if it might be a precursor to violence. Often, it was nothing. A delivery truck. A neighbor. His own overreaction, which he recognized but could not control. This false alarm response happened so frequently that Elena had begun to notice the way he flinched, the way his shoulders would bunch up toward his ears. She had stopped reaching out to touch him without warning; she had learned to announce herself when she approached from behind.

The touch itself had become intolerable. When Elena tried to hold his hand or put an arm around him, his first instinct was to pull away. He was not conscious of it—it happened before thought—but the consequence was that she had stopped trying. The intimacy of their marriage had become something he was avoiding without quite admitting it to himself. At work, he had begun to decline assignments that required him to be around other people for extended periods. He had stopped going to editorial meetings in person, sending his notes by email instead. His editor, who had been sympathetic after his return, was beginning to ask questions about his commitment to the job.

The alcohol smell was everywhere—in bars he passed, on the breath of colleagues at occasional office gatherings, in the hand sanitizer that contained ethanol and triggered the same cascade of dread. He had begun to avoid restaurants. He had stopped attending social events. What frightened him most was not just the memory itself, but the sense that his body had become a traitor, that it could be hijacked into terror by a smell or a sound or a touch that meant nothing at all.

It was Elena who finally insisted he see someone. She said it not unkindly, but with the firmness of someone who was watching her husband disappear into a cage of his own making. Marcus had resisted for months, telling himself that what he needed was time, that he was strong enough to push through. But he had come to understand, sitting in his apartment listening to the sounds of the city outside and feeling his body coil with readiness for threats that were not coming, that he was no longer the person who could simply endure. He had finally made the appointment because he could no longer bear the thought of losing Elena, or his career, or the small remaining pieces of the life he had fought so hard to keep alive in that basement.
